blocks.p: When the battle was over, everything in the camp was put in order. Then the captains and elders of Mansoul came together to greet Emmanuel while he was still outside the town; and they greeted him and welcomed him, with a thousand welcomes, because he had come to the borders of Mansoul again. He smiled on them and said, “Peace be to you.”

Then they set out for the town; they went up to Mansoul, the Prince and all the new forces he had now brought with him to the war. All the gates of the town were thrown open to receive him, so glad were they of his blessed return. And this was the manner and order of his entry into Mansoul.

First. As I said, all the gates of the town were set open, yes, and the gates of the castle too; and the elders of the town of Mansoul placed themselves at the gates of the town to greet him as he entered. And so they did; for as he drew near and approached the gates, they said, “Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall come in!” And others answered, “Who is the King of glory?” And they replied among themselves, “The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle! Lift up your heads, you gates; lift them up, you everlasting doors!” and so on through the psalm. [Ps. 24:7-9]

Second. It was also ordered by the people of Mansoul that all the way from the town gates to the gates of the castle, his blessed Majesty should be entertained with song by those who had the best skill in music in all the town. Then the elders and the rest of the men of Mansoul answered one another, as Emmanuel entered the town and until he came to the castle gates, with songs and the sound of trumpets, saying, “They have seen your goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, into the sanctuary. The singers went in front, the players on instruments followed after, and among them were the young women playing tambourines.” [Ps. 68:24-25]

Third. Then the captains (for I want to say a word about them) attended the Prince in their order as he entered the gates of Mansoul. Captain Credence went in front, and Captain Good-Hope with him; Captain Charity came behind with others of his companions, and Captain Patience followed after all; and the rest of the captains, some on the right hand and some on the left, accompanied Emmanuel into Mansoul. And all the while the colors were displayed, the trumpets sounded, and the soldiers kept up a continual shouting. The Prince himself rode into the town in his armor, which was all of beaten gold, and in his chariot. Its pillars were of silver, its floor of gold, its covering of purple, and its interior was paved with love for the daughters of the town of Mansoul.

Fourth. When the Prince came to the entrance of Mansoul, he found all the streets strewn with lilies and flowers, and finely decked with boughs and branches from the green trees that stood all around the town. Every doorway, too, was full of people, each of whom had decorated the front of his house with something rare and excellent to entertain him as he passed through the streets. And as Emmanuel passed by, they themselves welcomed him with shouts and cries of joy, saying, “Blessed be the Prince who comes in the name of his Father Shaddai!”

Fifth. At the castle gates the elders of Mansoul, namely, the Lord Mayor, the Lord Willbewill, the town’s own preacher, Mr. Knowledge, and Mr. Mind, with others of the gentry of the place, greeted Emmanuel again. They bowed before him, they kissed the dust of his feet; they thanked, they blessed, and they praised his Highness for not taking advantage of them for their sins, but instead taking pity on them in their misery and returning to them with mercies, to build up their Mansoul forever. Then he was brought straight up to the castle, for that was the royal palace and the place where his honor was to dwell. It had been made ready for his Highness by the presence of the Lord Secretary and the work of Captain Credence. So he entered in.

Sixth. Then the common people of the town of Mansoul came to him in the castle to mourn and weep and lament over their wickedness, by which they had driven him out of the town. When they came, they bowed themselves to the ground seven times; they wept, they wept aloud, and asked the Prince’s forgiveness, and prayed that he would once again, as in the old days, confirm his love to Mansoul.

To this the great Prince replied, “Do not weep, but go your way, eat the rich food and drink the sweet wine, and send portions to those who have nothing prepared; for the joy of your Lord is your strength. [Neh. 8:9-10] I have returned to Mansoul with mercies, and my name shall be set up, exalted, and magnified by it.” He also took these inhabitants and kissed them, and held them close to his heart.

Moreover, he gave the elders of Mansoul, and each officer of the town, a chain of gold and a signet ring. He also sent their wives earrings and jewels and bracelets and other things, and bestowed many precious things on the true-born children of Mansoul.

When Emmanuel the Prince had done all these things for the famous town of Mansoul, he said to them, “First wash your garments, then put on your ornaments, and then come to me in the castle of Mansoul.” So they went to the fountain that was set open for Judah and Jerusalem to wash in; and there they washed, and there they made their “garments white,” and came back to the Prince in the castle, and so they stood before him.

And now there was music and dancing throughout the whole town of Mansoul, because their Prince had once more given them his presence and the light of his face. The bells rang, too, and the sun shone warmly on them for a long while together.

The town of Mansoul now also set itself more thoroughly to seek the ruin of all the Diabolonians still remaining within its walls and in their dens in the town; for some of them had, to this day, escaped with life and limb from the hands of those set to suppress them.

But my Lord Willbewill was a greater terror to them now than he had ever been before, for his heart was now even more fully set to seek them out, track them down, and pursue them to the death. He hunted them night and day, and put them in sore distress, as will appear later.

When things had been set in order this far, the blessed Prince Emmanuel gave orders that the townsmen should without further delay appoint some to go out into the plain and bury the dead who lay there (the dead who fell by the sword of Emmanuel and by the shield of Captain Credence), so that the fumes and foul smells rising from them would not infect the air and trouble the famous town of Mansoul. There was another reason for this order as well: that, as far as it lay in Mansoul’s power, they might cut off the name and being and memory of those enemies from the thoughts of the town and its inhabitants.

So the Lord Mayor, that wise and trusty friend of the town of Mansoul, gave orders that men should be employed in this necessary business, with Mr. Godly-Fear and one Mr. Upright as overseers; and workers were put under them to bury the slain who lay dead in the plains. These were their tasks: some were to dig the graves, some to bury the dead, and some to go back and forth across the plains and all around the borders of Mansoul, to see whether a skull, or a bone, or a piece of a bone of a doubter could still be found above ground anywhere near the town. If any was found, the searchers were to set up a mark beside it, so that the buriers might find it and bury it out of sight; so that the name and memory of a Diabolonian doubter might be blotted out from under heaven, and the children, and those yet to be born in Mansoul, might not know, if possible, what a skull, or a bone, or a piece of a bone of a doubter was. So the buriers did as they were commanded: they buried the doubters, and all the skulls and bones and pieces of bones of doubters wherever they found them; and so they cleansed the plains. Now also Mr. God’s-Peace took up his commission again, and acted as in former days.

So they buried in the plains around Mansoul the Election-doubters, the Calling-doubters, the Grace-doubters, the Perseverance-doubters, the Resurrection-doubters, the Salvation-doubters, and the Glory-doubters. Their captains had been Captain Rage, Captain Cruel, Captain Damnation, Captain Insatiable, Captain Brimstone, Captain Torment, Captain No-Ease, Captain Sepulchre, and Captain Past-Hope; and old Incredulity, under Diabolus, was their general. There were also the seven heads of their army, and they were the Lord Beelzebub, the Lord Lucifer, the Lord Legion, the Lord Apollyon, the Lord Python, the Lord Cerberus, and the Lord Belial. But the princes and the captains, with old Incredulity their general, all made their escape; so it was their men who fell slain by the power of the Prince’s forces and by the hands of the men of the town of Mansoul. They were buried as I have told, to the exceedingly great joy of the now famous town of Mansoul. Those who buried them buried their arms with them, which were cruel instruments of death (their weapons were arrows, darts, mauls, firebrands, and the like). They buried their armor too, their colors and banners, with the standard of Diabolus, and whatever else they could find that so much as smelled of a Diabolonian doubter.

Now when the tyrant had arrived at Hell-Gate Hill with his old friend Incredulity, they went straight down into the den. And when they had grieved there a while with their fellows over their misfortune and their great loss before the town of Mansoul, they flew at last into a passion, and revenged they would be. So they immediately called a council to plot what more was to be done against the famous town of Mansoul. Their yawning bellies could not wait to see what came of the counsel their Lord Lucifer and their Lord Apollyon had given before; for their raging gullets thought every day as long as a short forever, until they were filled with the body and soul, the flesh and bones, and all the delicacies of Mansoul. They therefore resolved to make another attempt on the town of Mansoul, with an army made up partly of Doubters and partly of Bloodmen. Now take a more particular account of both.

The Doubters take their name from their nature, as well as from the land and kingdom where they are born. Their nature is to raise a question over every one of the truths of Emmanuel; and their country is called the land of Doubting. That land lies off to the north, farthest away of all, between the land of Darkness and the place called “the valley of the shadow of death.” For though the land of Darkness and the valley of the shadow of death are sometimes spoken of as if they were one and the same place, they are really two, lying only a little way apart, and the land of Doubting juts in and lies between them. This is the land of Doubting; and those who came with Diabolus to ruin the town of Mansoul were natives of that country.

The Bloodmen take their name from the malice of their nature, and from the fury in them to vent it on the town of Mansoul. Their land lies under the Dog Star, and their minds are ruled by it. The name of their country is the province of Loath-good. Its farthest parts lie far from the land of Doubting, yet both countries border on the hill called Hell-Gate Hill. These people are always in league with the Doubters, for together they call into question the faith and faithfulness of the men of the town of Mansoul; and so both are equally fit for their prince’s service.

Now out of these two countries, by the beating of his drum, Diabolus raised another army against the town of Mansoul, twenty-five thousand strong. There were ten thousand Doubters and fifteen thousand Bloodmen, and they were put under several captains for the war; and old Incredulity was again made general of the army.

As for the Doubters, their captains were five of the seven who had been heads of the last Diabolonian army, and these are their names: Captain Beelzebub, Captain Lucifer, Captain Apollyon, Captain Legion, and Captain Cerberus. Of the captains they had before, some were made lieutenants and some ensigns of the army.

But Diabolus did not expect the Doubters to prove his principal men in this expedition, for their manhood had been tested before, and the Mansoulians had beaten them. He brought them only to swell the numbers, and to help at a pinch if need be. His trust he put in his Bloodmen, for they were all rugged villains, and he knew what feats they had done before.

As for the Bloodmen, they too were under command, and the names of their captains were Captain Cain, Captain Nimrod, Captain Ishmael, Captain Esau, Captain Saul, Captain Absalom, Captain Judas, and Captain Pope.
1. Captain Cain was over two bands, namely, the zealous and the angry Bloodmen. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon, the emblem on his shield, was the murdering club.
2. Captain Nimrod was captain over two bands, namely, the tyrannical and the encroaching Bloodmen. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was the great bloodhound.
3. Captain Ishmael was captain over two bands, namely, the mocking and the scorning Bloodmen. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was one mocking at Abraham’s Isaac.

4. Captain Esau was captain over two bands, namely, the Bloodmen who begrudge another the blessing, and the Bloodmen who are for taking their private revenge on others. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was one lying in wait in secret to murder Jacob.

5. Captain Saul was captain over two bands, namely, the groundlessly jealous and the devilishly furious Bloodmen. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was three bloody darts hurled at harmless David.

6. Captain Absalom was captain over two bands, namely, the Bloodmen who will kill a father or a friend for the glory of this world, and those Bloodmen who will string a man along with fair words until they have run him through with their swords. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was the son pursuing his father’s blood.

7. Captain Judas was over two bands, namely, the Bloodmen who will sell a man’s life for money, and those also who will betray their friend with a kiss. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was thirty pieces of silver and the noose.

8. Captain Pope was captain over one band, for all these spirits are joined in one under him. His standard-bearer carried the red colors, and his escutcheon was the stake, the flame, and the good man in it.

Now the reason Diabolus rallied another force so soon after being beaten out of the field was that he put mighty confidence in these Bloodmen, far more than he had put in his Doubters, though the Doubters too had often done him great service in strengthening his kingdom. But these Bloodmen he had tested often, and their sword seldom came back empty. Besides, he knew that, like mastiffs, they would fasten on anyone: on father, mother, brother, sister, prince, or governor, yes, on the Prince of princes himself. And what encouraged him even more was that they had once forced Emmanuel out of the kingdom of Universe. “And why,” he thought, “may they not drive him from the town of Mansoul as well?”

So this army, twenty-five thousand strong, was led up against the town of Mansoul by their general, the great Lord Incredulity. Now Mr. Watch-well, the scoutmaster-general, went out to spy for himself, and brought Mansoul word of their coming. So they shut their gates and put themselves in a posture of defense against these new Diabolonians who were coming up against the town.
So Diabolus brought up his army and laid siege to the town of Mansoul. The Doubters were posted around Feel-gate, and the Bloodmen settled down before Eye-gate and Ear-gate.

When this army had encamped, Incredulity, in the name of Diabolus, in his own name, and in the name of the Bloodmen and the rest who were with him, sent Mansoul a summons as hot as a red-hot iron, demanding that they yield, and threatening that if they still held out against them, they would burn Mansoul down with fire at once. For you must understand that what the Bloodmen wanted was not so much that Mansoul should surrender as that she should be destroyed and cut off out of the land of the living. True, they sent to her to surrender; but even if she had, that would not have stanched or quenched these men’s thirst. They must have blood, the blood of Mansoul, or they die; and that is where they get their name. That is why Diabolus had kept these Bloodmen in reserve until now: so that when all his other engines had failed, they might be played against the town of Mansoul as his last and surest card.

When the townsmen received this red-hot summons, it stirred in them at first some shifting and wavering thoughts; but in less than half an hour they agreed together to carry the summons to the Prince. This they did, once they had written at the bottom of it, “Lord, save Mansoul from bloody men!”

So he took it, and looked at it, and considered it, and noticed also the short petition the men of Mansoul had written at the bottom. Then he called the noble Captain Credence to him and told him to take Captain Patience and go and take charge of the side of Mansoul besieged by the Bloodmen. So they did as they were commanded, and the two of them secured that side of Mansoul.

Then he commanded that Captain Good-Hope and Captain Charity and my Lord Willbewill should take charge of the other side of the town. “And I,” said the Prince, “will set my standard on the battlements of your castle; and you three, keep watch against the Doubters.” This done, he further commanded that the brave Captain Experience should draw up his men in the marketplace and drill them there day by day before the people of the town of Mansoul.

Now this siege was long, and the enemy made many a fierce attempt on the town of Mansoul, especially those called the Bloodmen; and some of the townsmen took many a hard knock from them, especially Captain Self-Denial, who, I should have told you before, had now been given charge of Ear-gate and Eye-gate against the Bloodmen. This Captain Self-Denial was a young man, but stout, and a native of Mansoul, as Captain Experience also was. Emmanuel, at his second return to Mansoul, had made him captain over a thousand of the Mansoulians, for the good of the town. So this captain, being a hardy man of great courage, willing to risk himself for the good of the town, would now and then sally out on the Bloodmen and give them many notable alarms. He fought several brisk skirmishes with them and did some execution among them; but you must understand that this could not be done without his taking some knocks himself, for he carried several of their marks on his face, yes, and some on other parts of his body.

So, after some time spent in the trial of the faith and hope and love of the town of Mansoul, the Prince Emmanuel one day called his captains and men of war together and divided them into two companies. This done, he commanded them, at an appointed time and very early in the morning, to sally out on the enemy.

“Let half of you fall on the Doubters,” he said, “and half of you fall on the Bloodmen. Those of you who go out against the Doubters, kill and slay, and cause to perish as many of them as you can by any means lay hands on. But you who go out against the Bloodmen, do not slay them; take them alive.”

So at the appointed time, early in the morning, the captains went out as they were commanded. Captain Good-Hope, Captain Charity, and those who were joined with them, such as Captain Innocent and Captain Experience, went out against the Doubters; and Captain Credence and Captain Patience, with Captain Self-Denial and the rest who were to join them, went out against the Bloodmen.

Now those who went out against the Doubters drew up in a body before the plain and marched on to give them battle. But the Doubters, remembering how they had fared last time, retreated, not daring to stand the shock, and fled from the Prince’s men. So they pursued them and killed many in the pursuit, but they could not catch them all. Of those who escaped, some went home; and the rest went straggling up and down the country like vagrants, by fives and nines and seventeens, and there practiced many of their Diabolonian deeds on the barbarous people. Nor did these people rise up in arms against them, but let themselves be enslaved by them. After this the Doubters would also show themselves in companies before the town of Mansoul, but never stay there; for if Captain Credence, Captain Good-Hope, or Captain Experience so much as showed himself, they fled.

Those who went out against the Bloodmen did as they were commanded: they held back from killing any, and tried instead to surround them. But the Bloodmen, when they saw that no Emmanuel was in the field, concluded that no Emmanuel was in Mansoul either; so they regarded what the captains were doing as, in their words, the fruit of their wild and foolish fancies, and despised them rather than feared them. But the captains kept to their business and at last surrounded them; and those who had routed the Doubters came in at full speed to help. So in the end, after a little struggling (for the Bloodmen would have run for it too, only now it was too late; for though they are mischievous and cruel where they can get the upper hand, all Bloodmen are chicken-hearted once they see themselves matched and equaled), the captains took them and brought them to the Prince.
Now when they had been taken, brought before the Prince, and examined, he found that they came from three different counties, though they all came out of one land.
1. One sort came out of Blind-man-shire, and they were those who did what they did in ignorance.
2. Another sort came out of Blind-zeal-shire, and they did what they did out of superstition.
3. The third sort came out of the town of Malice, in the county of Envy, and they did what they did out of spite and implacable hatred.

As for the first, those who came out of Blind-man-shire: when they saw where they were, and against whom they had fought, they trembled and cried as they stood before him; and as many of these as asked him for mercy, he touched their lips with his golden scepter.

Those who came out of Blind-zeal-shire did not do as their fellows did. They argued that they had a right to do what they had done, because Mansoul was a town whose laws and customs were different from those of everyone who lived around it. Very few of these could be brought to see their evil; but those who did, and asked for mercy, also obtained favor.

But those who came out of the town of Malice, in the county of Envy, neither wept, nor argued, nor repented, but stood before him gnawing their tongues in anguish and fury, because they could not have their will on Mansoul. Now these last, and all those of the other two sorts who did not sincerely ask pardon for their crimes, he bound over under sufficient bond to answer for what they had done against Mansoul and against her King at the great general assizes, the high court to be held for our Lord the King, where he himself shall appoint, for the country and kingdom of Universe. So each man was bound for himself to come in when called upon, and answer before our Lord the King for what he had done.
And that is all concerning this second army that Diabolus sent to overthrow Mansoul.
